themes.theme: Registries of AI systems and algorithms for public administrations
themes.definition: Proposed EU and national registries of algorithms used in the public sector, and the Commission's internal register of the AI systems it uses.
themes.what_is_set_out: The JRC handbook returns to registries several times: a European registry of AI algorithms federating national registries 'to monitor the development and market around AI' (#141, offered as an option that 'could be taken into consideration'); the same idea as a recommended action, to monitor the digital transformation of the public sector and share information (#163); registries built from catalogues of AI applications such as the AI-on-demand platform, coordinated by the living-in.EU movement (#148); and an 'EU united AI registry' based on national and local registries that links reusable algorithms, models and datasets (#155). Per the coder note on #141, the registry is not framed as mandatory registration or as publication for accountability, and no holder is named. The one register of tools actually in use is internal to the Commission: the ISG-AI and corporate governance boards must 'establish and maintain an up-to-date register of AI systems in use at the Commission, assessed against corporate guidelines and legal requirements' from Q2 2024 (#283), alongside a list of AI initiatives with proposed priorities (#284); publication of either is not stated.
themes.holders: JRC registries: holder not stated (living-in.EU coordinates activities in #148). Commission register: the ISG-AI, the AI@EC Network and corporate governance boards.
themes.binding: JRC: suggestions and recommendations with no named holder. AIatEC: internal Commission mandate with a timeline (Q2 2024, then continuous or quarterly). No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Commission register (#283): trigger, inclusion in the register (from Q2 2024, then continuously); compared against, 'corporate guidelines and legal requirements'; metric or threshold, not stated; who, the ISG-AI and corporate governance boards; what happens with the result, not stated. The JRC registries are for monitoring and reuse, not for checking tools.

quotes.quote: Setting up a European registry of AI algorithms by federating and promoting the creation of national registries to monitor the development and market around AI and help in meeting the relevant criteria set down by EU regulations.
Build an EU united AI registry based on national and local AI registries , adding (when available) the information and linking to the reusable parts involved: algorithms, models and datasets.
Establish and maintain an up-to-date register of AI systems in use at the Commission, assessed against corporate guidelines and legal requirements .
Establish and maintain a list of existing AI initiatives and propose their prioritisation in view of the creation of corporate AI services.

themes.theme: Shared repositories, reusable components and data spaces
themes.definition: Proposed shared infrastructure through which public administrations reuse AI components, standards and data.
themes.what_is_set_out: The JRC handbook says that in developing AI solutions, reuse and sharing of components with other public administrations on open repositories 'should be privileged', following existing EU building blocks (#153), with directories aligned to policy areas so operators can reuse components elsewhere in Europe (#154) and national repositories of standards, guidelines and performance metrics (#156); its proposed EU AI registry would link reusable algorithms, models and datasets (#155). It also proposes a Common European Data Space for public administrations that includes data from private actors and, per the note, 'should not be a central repository' (#147), says dedicated data spaces should grant the conditions for data access and governance (#150), and calls for reference organisations for data trusts and data cooperatives (#151, which the coders flagged as only indirectly relevant). The Commission's internal plan includes a framework to reuse, and contribute to, open-source AI (#282).
themes.holders: Public administrations developing AI and GovTech initiatives (JRC, often not named); operators of data spaces (not named); the ISG-AI, DIGIT and corporate governance boards (Commission).
themes.binding: Recommendations and suggestions (JRC); an internal Commission action (AIatEC). No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Performance metrics are proposed for national repositories (#156) but not defined, and their use in evaluating tools is not stated (coder note).

quotes.quote: For the development of AI solutions reuse and sharing of components with other public administrations on open repositories should be privileged, following the existing building blocks and guidelines developed within the relevant EU initiatives.

Promote the implementation of a Common European Data Space 63 dedicated to public administrations providing not only data collected by the public sector, but also other relevant data acquired from both established and emerging actors

Aligning components specifications to the areas they address (e.g., transportation, housing, etc.), so that dedicated directories would help operators reuse existing component in other parts of Europe.
Develop a framework to reuse (and contribute to) open -source AI, also in line with the Commission’s strategy on open -source software

themes.theme: Proposed networks, observatories and learning communities for public-sector AI
themes.definition: EU-level groups, observatories, alliances and partnerships proposed to connect public administrations with each other and with researchers on AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The JRC handbook proposes starting with 'a coordinated governance approach' to identify, discuss and 'regulate' common values, without naming any body (#140); a European AI Working Group dedicated to the public sector (#142), with Member States designating national organisations to represent public-sector AI in it and coordinate their own administrations (#143); a shared mechanism for producing learning material (#144); links between national, local and cross-border experimentation facilities (#145); a research and knowledge alliance of universities working with the public sector (#146); networks of local digital twins (#149, which the coders flagged as promoting adoption); and an EU observatory on AI in the public sector as a hub joining national observatories (#160, #162), kept up to date by stakeholders (#161) and coordinated with the OECD and UNESCO (#164). It also says Member States 'can and should learn from the successes and failures' of national AI strategies (#138). The later JRC report suggests the AI Board sub-configuration as a forum for AI literacy across public administrations (#251), asks national and local administrations to mobilise EU funding and guidance and avoid fragmentation (#252), and says networks and partnerships 'can facilitate knowledge sharing and resource pooling' (#259). Almost all are options ('could', 'it is suggested') with no named holder, and none is established by these documents.
themes.holders: Mostly not stated; Member States (#138, #143, #162); stakeholders (#161); national and local administrations (#252); the AI Board sub-configuration as a possible forum (#251).
themes.binding: Non-binding: suggestions and recommendations in JRC reports. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: n/a. The handbook's call for monitoring concerns the uptake of national strategies (#138), not the outputs of tools.

quotes.quote: Setting up an Artificial Intelligence Working Group at European level specifically dedicated to the public sector.
Member States should identify organisations at the national level to represent AI in the public sector within the EU Working Group.

An EU observatory on AI dedicated to the public sector could be set up. It would act as central hub of expertise to establish a community of practice, while joining up national observatories around Europe
Establishing strong support systems and networks, including partnerships with other organisations and stakeholders, can facilitate knowledge sharing and resource pooling.

themes.theme: Internal AI governance bodies, networks and task forces within EU institutions
themes.definition: Bodies, networks and cross-functional arrangements that EU institutions set up, or are told to set up, to coordinate their own use of AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission's AI@EC communication creates an Interservice Steering Group on AI led by DIGIT with a director-level core group of DGT, OP, HR, CNECT, the Secretariat-General and the JRC (#281), 'in charge of coordinating and implementing the AI@EC initiative and overseeing' the AI@EC Network (#288); the Network, led by DGT, is a Commission-wide community of users, staff and experts for sharing information, raising awareness and finding joint projects (#280, #287), and a change-management and communication framework for staff is planned (#286), alongside the internal register and list of initiatives (#283, #284). The European Parliament's 2024 framework, awaiting Bureau approval per the coder note on #178, sets up a Governance Board including the ICT services and key administration representatives (#181) that approves the AI roadmap and ensures 'transversal involvement' of services and end users (#180) and establishes a network of AI business partners (#183); the roadmap is drafted by the ICT services with the Inter-DG network (#182). The ECA's Advisory Committee on AI advises on compliance, coordinates risk assessment and management and acts as internal expert (#272), and the ECA commits that 'all ECA stakeholders collaborate in a coordinated way' (#278). The EDPS tells EU institutions that controllers should liaise with the DPO, Legal Service, IT Service and Local Informatics Security Officer (#224), that an AI task force including the DPO, with an action plan, 'may contribute' (#225), and that procurement and deployment staff should coordinate (#216). The bodies differ in power: the Parliament's Board approves, the ISG-AI oversees, the ECA's committee advises, and the EDPS arrangements are suggestions.
themes.holders: The Commission's ISG-AI, DIGIT, DGT and the AI@EC Network; the European Parliament's Governance Board, ICT services and Inter-DG network; the ECA and its Advisory Committee on AI; controllers in EU institutions with their DPO, legal, IT and security functions.
themes.binding: Internal mandates (Commission, ECA); a proposed internal framework using 'shall' (European Parliament 2024); recommendations and encouragement (EDPS). No consequence stated.
themes.checks: n/a, except that the ECA committee coordinates 'the assessment and management of risks' (#272) and the Commission register is assessed against guidelines and law (#283, see the registries theme); neither states a comparator for outputs, a metric or what happens with the result.

quotes.quote: The Steering Group is in charge of coordinating and implementing the AI@EC initiative and overseeing the activities of the AI@EC Network.
It shall approve the AI roadmap as well as ensure a transversal involvement of the administration's services and end users.

quotes.location: AI governance at the ECA, para 17 (p. 7)
quotes.quote: Its core responsibilities include advising on institutional compliance with the regulatory framework governing the use of AI, coordinating the assessment and management of risks, and acting as an internal expert on AI-related matters.
controllers should liaise with all relevant functions within the organisation, notably the DPO, Legal Service, the IT Service and the Local Informatics Security Officer (LISO)

themes.theme: Cooperation between EU institutions and with peer bodies on AI use
themes.definition: Arrangements by which an EU institution relies on, aligns with or learns from other institutions and peer bodies in its own use of AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The ECA's strategy treats the Commission as a supplier: the ECA 'will define and communicate our functional and security requirements' so that tools meet the standards of audit work (#274) and will work with the Commission team to tailor Commission tools to its needs (#276). It also commits to align its data classification policy with its auditees, 'especially the European Commission', so that classification stays consistent across exchanges and AI processing (#273), to align its practice with emerging EU-wide standards (#277), and to cooperate with other supreme audit institutions through INTOSAI and EUROSAI (#275). The Commission's AI@EC plan asks its internal AI support to work 'in close liaison with the future AI Office' (#279) and to seek knowledge sharing and cooperation with other EU institutions, bodies and agencies and with Member States from Q3 2024 (#285). [inference] An auditor that relies on tools supplied by the body it audits, and aligns its classification with that body, faces an independence question that the passages do not address.
themes.holders: The European Court of Auditors; the Commission team supplying tools; other supreme audit institutions; the Commission's ISG-AI, AI@EC Network and DIGIT; the AI Office.
themes.binding: Institutional commitments ('will', 'essential'); internal instructions ('should') and an internal mandate with a timeline. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Requirements for tools (#274): trigger, adoption of Commission-provided tools; compared against, the ECA's functional and security requirements; metric, not stated; who, the ECA defines the requirements and works with the Commission team; result, tailoring of the tools (#276). This is a requirement on tools, not a check of their outputs.

quotes.quote: we will define and communicate our functional and security requirements to ensure that tools meet the standards necessary for our audit work.

We will co-operate with other supreme audit institutions, taking advantage of existing working groups (INTOSAI, EUROSAI, etc.), to build on their experience and knowledge in the field of public audit.

It is equally essential to review and enhance our data classification policy, to ensure that it is consistent (on AI and other aspects) with the policies of our auditees, especially the European Commission
This should happen in close liaison with the future AI Office in the European Commission, which will play a key role in the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act.

themes.theme: Data protection referrals: DPO advice and prior consultation of the EDPS
themes.definition: Routes within the EU institutions' data protection regime by which a controller using AI must or should seek advice from its data protection officer or consult the EDPS.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS risk guidance says that, in the case it describes, an EU institution 'would have to prior consult the EDPS pursuant to Article 40(1) EUDPR' (#221), and the generative-AI orientations put it plainly: 'If risks that cannot be mitigated by reasonable means are identified, it is time to consult the EDPS' (#229). Inside the institution, the controller 'is obliged to seek the advice of the DPO when carrying out a DPIA' (#227), and the DPO 'should be involved' in reviewing data-sharing agreements with model providers (#226), though per the coder note the DPO advises and has no authority. These are the only referrals in this cell in which a public body that uses AI must go to a supervisor about its own deployment.
themes.holders: EU institutions as controllers; their DPOs; the EDPS as recipient of prior consultation.
themes.binding: Statutory under the EU institutions' data protection regulation (Art. 40(1) prior consultation, #221; the controller is 'obliged' to seek DPO advice, #227); the orientations' conclusion box uses non-binding phrasing (#229); DPO involvement in agreements is recommended (#226). What follows from a consultation is not stated.
themes.checks: The data protection impact assessment is the check here. Trigger: carrying out a DPIA (#227), with referral when risks 'cannot be mitigated by reasonable means' (#229). Compared against: data protection risks. Metric or threshold: residual risk that cannot be mitigated by reasonable means; no measure is given. Who: the controller with the DPO's advice, then the EDPS. What happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: In that case, the EUI would have to prior consult the EDPS pursuant to Article 40(1) EUDPR.
If risks that cannot be mitigated by reasonable means are identified, it is time to consult the EDPS.
The controller is obliged to seek the advice of the DPO when carrying out a DPIA.

quotes.location: PDF p.15 (printed p.14), s.5 Role of DPOs
quotes.quote: the DPO should be involved in the review of compliance issues in the context of data sharing agreements signed with model providers.

themes.theme: Involving stakeholders, affected people, end-users, workers and citizens
themes.definition: Mechanisms that bring people outside the developing or deploying team (affected groups, experts, civil society, workers, end-users, citizens) into decisions about an AI tool.
themes.what_is_set_out: An AI Act recital says deployers carrying out a fundamental-rights impact assessment, 'in particular when AI systems are used in the public sector, could involve relevant stakeholders', including representatives of affected groups, independent experts and civil society (#042), and another asks providers to document their risk-management choices and, where relevant, involve experts and external stakeholders (#030). The one 'shall' comes from other law: the prohibited-practices guidelines note that under EU employment law employers 'shall also consult with workers or their representatives' before introducing emotion recognition for medical or safety reasons, and that without this 'such systems cannot be introduced by reference to the AI Act as such' (#123 and #137 are the same footnote extracted by two coders). The EDPS says it 'may be appropriate' to seek the views of affected people or their representatives in a DPIA (#228) and suggests feedback loops 'where users can report issues or anomalies in inferences' (#218). The European Parliament's proposed framework says use cases 'must be identified, tested and validated through an inclusive process, involving the end-users' (#178), and its Governance Board ensures end-user involvement (#180). The JRC documents recommend co-creation with citizens (#139), attention to the representativeness of the citizens involved to avoid biased input (#166), civic engagement (#165) and public outreach (#254).
themes.holders: Deployers of high-risk AI (public sector named); providers; employers; EU institutions as controllers (holder often not stated); the European Parliament administration and its Governance Board; public administrations and Member States (JRC, holder often not stated).
themes.binding: Mostly permissive or recommended ('could', 'may be appropriate', 'should', 'strongly recommended'); a statutory duty under employment law, restated in a footnote, with a stated consequence (the system cannot be introduced by reference to the AI Act); 'must' in the European Parliament's internal framework, pending approval.
themes.checks: Two passages concern checking a tool with its users. Use-case validation (#178): trigger, before use cases are adopted; compared against, not stated; metric, not stated; who, holder not stated, with end-users involved; result, not stated. Feedback loops (#218): trigger, ongoing use; compared against, users' reports of 'issues or anomalies in inferences'; metric, not stated; who, users report and the holder who acts is not stated; result, per the note, used to identify data-quality problems or drift and 'make necessary adjustments'.

quotes.quote: in particular when AI systems are used in the public sector, could involve relevant stakeholders, including the representatives of groups of persons likely to be affected by the AI system, independent experts, and civil society organisations
In conformity with EU employment law, if such new technologies are introduced, employers shall also consult with workers or their representatives, conform national procedures.
Create feedback loops where users can report issues or anomalies in inferences.

quotes.location: p. 2 (=== page 2), Section II, 'Scope: AI at the…
quotes.quote: Relevant use cases must be identified, tested and validated through an inclusive process, involving the end-users.

themes.theme: Remote biometric identification by law enforcement: notification, delegation and national laws
themes.definition: Coordination arrangements around law-enforcement use of remote biometric identification under the Article 5(1)(h) exceptions, as the prohibited-practices guidelines describe them.
themes.what_is_set_out: This is the cell's clearest case of a public body, as deployer, holding coordination duties. Each use of a remote biometric identification system for one of the Article 5(1)(h) objectives 'must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority', after each use (#127; #122 is the same paragraph), and per the coder note these notices feed the authorities' annual reports to the Commission. Where another entity, including a private party, acts 'on behalf of' a law-enforcement authority (#124), it 'will have to contribute to the preparation of the FRIA with all relevant information' (#125), while the impact assessment itself stays with the deployer. The systems are registered in a non-public section of the EU database (#126); national laws authorising such use must be notified to the Commission within 30 days (#129), drafts may be sent in advance (#128), and the guidelines suggest that national law describe 'any cooperation with private or public authorities, including in other countries, and data transfers and exchanges' (#130).
themes.holders: Law-enforcement authorities as deployers; entities or persons acting on their behalf, including private parties; Member States (national law); market surveillance and data protection authorities and the Commission as recipients.
themes.binding: Statutory duties restated in non-binding Commission guidelines ('must', 'will have to'); suggested content for national law; encouragement for draft laws. Non-notification of national laws within 30 days is treated as missing the legal deadline (#129); no other consequence stated.
themes.checks: The per-use notification is a record, not a test of outputs: trigger, each use; content, per the note, at minimum the Article 5(6) information and no sensitive operational data; recipients, the market surveillance and data protection authorities; what they do with it beyond annual reporting, not stated. The fundamental-rights impact assessment (#125): trigger, not stated in the passage; who, the deployer, with information from those acting on its behalf; comparator, metric and use of results not stated here.

quotes.quote: Each use of an RBI system pursuing one of the objectives listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) AI Act must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority.
‘On behalf of’ means that a law enforcement authority has delegated the performance of a law enforcement activity (or part of it) to another entity or person, including private parties

If other actors are acting on behalf of the deployer/the law enforcement authority, they will have to contribute to the preparation of the FRIA with all relevant information to ensure it is properly carried out.
the description of any cooperation with private or public authorities, including in other countries, and data transfers and exchanges;

themes.definition: Links between the Commission, ENISA, Member States, EU bodies and industry on the cybersecurity of AI and on AI-related cyber incidents.
themes.what_is_set_out: An AI Act recital asks the Commission to cooperate with ENISA on cybersecurity of AI systems (#034). ENISA's paper on frontier AI says ENISA 'aims to' refine its recommendations in close cooperation with Member States and EU institutions, bodies and agencies and align them with a forthcoming Commission Action Plan (#213); it recommends that governments integrate industry into crisis planning, with surge capacity, prioritisation and escalation frameworks and stress tests of multi-incident scenarios (#214), and that existing European and national initiatives on using AI models for cybersecurity be built on (#215). Per the coder note, #214 concerns incidents accelerated by attackers' use of AI, an edge case for the governance of public-sector tools.
themes.holders: The Commission and ENISA; ENISA with Member States and EU institutions, bodies and agencies; governments; holder not stated (#215).
themes.binding: Recital ('should'); recommendations; a statement of intention. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: n/a. The stress-testing in #214 is of crisis plans, not of AI tools or their outputs.

quotes.quote: the Commission should cooperate with ENISA on issues related to cybersecurity of AI systems.
ENISA aims to further refine and expand these recommendations in close cooperation with Member States and EUIBAs and will align these to upcoming European Commission Action Plan.

Governments should act and integrate industry into its crisis planning, establishing surge capacity models, defining clear prioritisation and escalation frameworks, and stress-testing multi-incident scenarios.

themes.definition: Links between EU actors and third-country regulators, international agreements and international organisations on AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission and Member States may exchange confidential information with third-country regulators where agreements guarantee an adequate level of confidentiality (#015). The Commission should pursue mutual recognition agreements on conformity assessment with third countries (#048), whose relevance to public-sector tools the coder note calls indirect. The prohibited-practices guidelines say parties to international law-enforcement and judicial cooperation agreements 'should make utmost efforts' to align them with the AI Act when they are revised or concluded (#132). The JRC handbook recommends that an EU observatory coordinate with the OECD and UNESCO on ethics and trustworthiness to avoid duplication (#164). Elsewhere in the cell, codes of practice must take international approaches into account (#089) and the ECA will work through INTOSAI and EUROSAI (#275).
themes.holders: The Commission and Member States; contracting parties to international agreements; the proposed EU observatory (not named).
themes.binding: Statutory power ('may'); recital and guidelines ('should', 'utmost efforts'); recommendation. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: The Commission and Member States may exchange, where necessary and in accordance with relevant provisions of international and trade agreements, confidential information with regulatory authorities of third countries
the Commission should actively explore possible international instruments for that purpose and in particular pursue the conclusion of mutual recognition agreements with third countries.

When those international agreements are revised or new ones are concluded in the future, the contracting parties should make utmost efforts to align those agreements with the requirements of th e AI Act.
Coordination with international organisations already operating in this area (e.g., OECD84, UNESCO 85) on critical topics like ethics and trustworthiness

absences: All seven starting codes for Coordination have passages: contact points, notifications, shared templates, registers and databases, supplier contracts, cross-government groups and networks, and referrals between bodies. 'Shared templates' is thin: only the simplified technical-documentation form, the Annex XIV code list and the training-data Summary template, with benchmarks and 'performance metrics' named but undefined. What a reader would expect and does not find: (1) any mechanism that carries the results of checks on a public body's AI outputs (error rates, review findings, consistency over repeated runs) to another public body, a supplier or a regulator, apart from per-use notification of remote biometric identification and the EDPS's suggested user feedback loops; (2) any shared template, benchmark set or method for testing or evaluating outputs; (3) any duty on a provider to tell a public deployer about a change of model version, prompt or configuration (model versions appear only as a field in the training-data Summary template, and corrective-action notices are the nearest equivalent), and nothing at all on prompts, configuration or confidence scores; (4) any coordination about which cases reach a human; (5) an established network of public bodies as users of AI (as distinct from regulators) at EU or Member State level: the JRC's working group, observatory and registries remain proposals, and the Commission, Parliament and ECA bodies are internal; (6) a contact point through which an affected person can reach a public-sector deployer about a specific tool, beyond the market surveillance single point of contact 'vis-à-vis the public'; (7) coordination between public bodies that use the same tool or supplier; and (8) consequences for failing to coordinate, which are almost never stated.
cross_cutting: Numbers with # in this file and parts 1 and 2 are passage IDs (EU-COO-DES-nnn). The cell is dominated by the AI Act and its Omnibus amendments, which set out a regulator-centred architecture: notifications, referrals and mutual assistance between market surveillance authorities, the AI Office and the Commission; the Board as an advisory forum with sub-groups; the notified-body network; sandbox and real-world-testing cooperation; and links to fundamental-rights and data protection authorities. A second large cluster runs along the supply chain (information duties, written supplier agreements, Article 50 marking and detection arrangements) from model and system providers towards deployers, and a third covers EU institutions' own internal bodies, the EDPS's procurement and referral advice, and the JRC's proposals for public-sector networks, registries and observatories. The AI Act duties are statutory 'shall', but are often qualified 'as appropriate' or framed as duties to 'facilitate' with no stated content, and almost no passage says what happens if a duty is not met; the Board's outputs are advice; the JRC material is entirely optional; the institutions' arrangements are internal mandates, the Parliament's still awaiting approval. The holders are overwhelmingly regulators and providers: public bodies appear as deployers holding coordination duties only in a few places (per-use notification of remote biometric identification, the EDPS's procurement and data-protection referrals for EU institutions, and the Commission's, Parliament's and ECA's internal governance), and one Omnibus passage makes a public authority's own AI system the object of AI Office enforcement (#199). On checking outputs, the coordination channels in this cell carry findings of non-compliance, documentation and declared performance rather than the results of checks on outputs; the closest passages are the provider's declared performance metrics in the instructions for use (#033), the EDPS advice to request metrics for evaluation against the organisation's objectives (#220), user feedback loops on anomalies and drift (#218), reliance on upstream testing of marking and detection solutions (#243), sandbox exit reports taken into account in conformity assessment (#093), testing at the request of fundamental-rights bodies (#013) and a possible common approach for external model evaluators (#264). None states an accuracy threshold, a check of consistency or repeatability, or anything on prompts, configuration or confidence scores, and model versions appear only as a documentation field (#211).
